title: Robinhood supports agent trading, but Codex says it can’t place trades—what am I missing?
author: HistoricalBag324
selftext:
I’m trying to get automated stock trading working with **Codex + Robinhood**, using cron jobs or scheduled tasks.

I can define the trading rules myself. What I’m trying to figure out is the execution part: how to have Codex check those conditions on a schedule and place buy/sell orders when they’re met.

Robinhood’s official Agentic documentation explicitly mentions agents placing orders and automating trading strategies. But whenever I ask Codex about setting this up, it keeps telling me it can only help with monitoring, paper trading, or alerts—not execute real trades through MCP or scheduled tasks.

Honestly, I’m confused. Robinhood is describing this as something agents can do, while Codex keeps saying it can’t.

I’m **not looking to switch platforms**. I specifically want to understand whether and how this works with Codex.

Has anyone here actually set up Codex to execute trades through Robinhood Agentic? Is there a supported integration or configuration I’m missing, or does Codex currently restrict this even though Robinhood supports it?

I’m not asking for trading strategies or ways around restrictions. I just want to understand what’s supported and, if it’s possible, how to get the automation running.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Codex in the chat window and Codex running on a cron are different animals. the chat one refuses on its own rules and no amount of asking gets past that. the scheduled version doesn't need the model to place anything. a script holds the Robinhood key, checks your rules on the schedule, and calls the order endpoint itself. the model, if you use it at all, decides yes or no and the script does the rest.

that's also the setup I'd want anyway. the model shouldn't hold the key that can open a position, because one day it reads something that convinces it to.

before it touches the real account, run the same script against a paper desk for a few weeks. my own desk covers that stage, Quantradin, at quantradin.com, and I built it around agents: an agent connects over MCP, trades paper with real fills, and you see what your rules actually did before money's on the line. no charge.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
One safe way to structure this is to keep Codex or another model on the proposal side and put the Robinhood credential and order submission behind a small deterministic service. That service should enforce position and loss limits, stale-data checks, idempotency, duplicate-order protection, an approval or kill switch, and explicit terminal states. Run the same scheduled loop against paper first, and log the point-in-time inputs, model and tool calls, proposed action, broker response, and failures so you can replay the decision later.

Disclosure: I work on Leroy, and if you are separating research from execution, it is worth checking out Leroy's MCP and wake feature. The MCP is useful for current context and historical evidence, while a wake can send an agent a signed evidence packet when a rule is met. It does not place orders, so the Robinhood execution boundary still needs to stay in your own controlled service.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
I can't confirm how Robinhood's agent docs interact with Codex's restrictions, so treat this as a general answer. Check Robinhood's current docs for the exact permissions.

Two separate things could be in play. Robinhood may support agent-placed orders on its side, while the tool you're running the agent in (Codex) has its own guardrails on real-money execution. Those are independent, so the docs from one don't override the other. The quickest test is a minimal script that calls Robinhood's API directly with your own credentials, scheduled with cron. That shows whether the block is Robinhood's or Codex's.

If you do go live, keep the LLM out of the execution path. Have it write and review the rules, but let a deterministic script place orders with hard limits: max position size, max daily loss, and a kill switch. Paper trade it for a few weeks first.

One rule worth building in early is a stand-down window around earnings and macro releases (CPI, FOMC). Scheduled jobs that fire into those windows get bad fills. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing for exactly this, so the script can check "is there an event in the next N minutes?" instead of parsing headlines.

Are you planning market or limit orders? That changes the risk a lot.
